subsubtopic: SUGGESTION BILL NOT BE DEALT WITH BUT RETURNED TO COMMITTEE FOR FURTHER STUDY-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity pursuant to Standing Order 43. Yesterday the Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Marchand) announced that the government had seen the merits of the argument put by the official opposition on behalf of western grain producers and was reconsidering the need for the metric measures "tonne" and "hectare". We were distressed to hear that the bill would not be amended but that proclamation would be delayed for an indeterminate period. Because we believe the House should not be asked to waste its time debating provisions which may or may not be proclaimed, and because we think it repugnant to be asked to provide government negotiators with the power to blackmail producers, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers):
That this House declines to deal with legislation which may not be proclaimed, and requests that the metric conversion bill be returned to committee so that further testimony may be heard and ill-advised provisions deleted.

subsubtopic: YOUTH UNEMPLOYMENT-REQUEST FOR MEASURES TO REDUCE LEVEL-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In light of the study released today by Statistics Canada which projects scandalously high and growing levels of youth unemployment as a result of nearly 500,000 full-time students entering the labour force this summer, and since we already have a national official youth unemployment rate of 15.6 per cent, giving Canada the highest
level of youth unemployment among the industrialized countries of the world, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the Minister of Manpower and Immigration be instructed to prepare and table in this House as soon as possible a comprehensive plan of action designed to reduce the level of youth unemployment; that this plan should include details of specific programs for relieving youth unemployment, job creation budgets and the projected job creation impact of the programs; and that these details include targeted levels of reduction in youth unemployment over the next five years and the means which the government proposes to use to reach those targets.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I seek the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of the fact that all the members of the Canadian Life Insurance Association who have written to me strongly oppose the new budget proposals the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) brought forward on March 31 concerning the taxation of life insurance death benefits, on the ground that these proposals are unfair to those who prefer to provide themselves for the financial security of their families through life insurance policies rather than let governments support them, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte):

subsubtopic: REASON FOR DELAY IN PUBLICATION OF REPORT ON PROBABILITY OF OIL SPILLS IN ARCTIC WATERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment. It relates to a report sponsored by his department entitled "Determination of probabilities of oil spills in Canadian Arctic waters". I thank the minister's office for having made a copy of this report available to me last night. The report, which the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development denied ever seeing when he replied to questions in the House last Friday, indicates blow-out probabilities in the Arctic in connection with our drilling there and makes numerous recommendations to deal with the risk. Can the minister explain why the report was not made known to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development at least before last Friday, particularly when it was apparently delivered to the Department of the Environment on or about March 28, over five weeks ago, and in particular because it is the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development who has the responsibility for agreeing to summer drilling permits in the Beaufort Sea area.

speakeroldname: Hon. Romeo LeBlanc (Minister of Fisheries and the Environment):
subsubtopic: REASON FOR DELAY IN PUBLICATION OF REPORT ON PROBABILITY OF OIL SPILLS IN ARCTIC WATERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development did not know of the report, he was in exactly the same position I was. I knew that a report had been commissioned some time ago, but I did not know that the report was ready. I do not know the exact delivery date. I took notice of the report when I came to this House on either this past Monday or Friday of last week. Therefore, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development was in exactly the same position as I was.
I might say to the hon. member that the reason the report was not immediately made available is that it has not yet been translated-that is why I cannot table it. It was in these circumstances that I circulated copies to those members who are interested. It is not a secret report. It was being made ready for publication and release.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: SUGGESTION PRESIDENT CARTER BE ASKED TO EXTEND DATE FOR DECISION ON NORTHERN PIPELINE

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration. Some recent but only partial national information from Statistics Canada indicate that there will be more than 120,000 young Canadians joining the work force this year who will not find job opportunities available to them and will
May 4, 1977

be joining the 400,000 young unemployed Canadians. Will the minister now tell the House whether he has any long-term strategy to provide young Canadians with meaningful, longterm and secure job opportunities and not just band-aid measures?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bud Cullen (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
subsubtopic: YOUTH UNEMPLOYMENT-MEASURES TO PROVIDE LONG-TERM JOBS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member should not concentrate only on the short-term measures that have already been announced. There are funds under Young Canada Works, the Student Summer Employment Assistance Program, the JET program with summer and winter components. In addition to that, under our Careers Canada, Careers Provinces and Choices, we are endeavouring to bridge the gap between the two, between leaving school and entering the work force, by giving the kind of counselling, training and in some cases job experience that is needed by young people to help them get into the work force.
In addition to that, I have had the opportunity to visit with my counterparts in both Italy and France to see if they had come up with any new ideas or something on a permanent basis that might be useful. Senator Humphrey in the United States has highlighted his own particular bill with the fact that this is not a parochial or local problem but is a national problem to all western industrialized societies.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Mr. Speaker, in order to be sure that I fully understand the question which the hon. member put to me yesterday, I would like him to be more specific, giving me details as to the area in British Columbia to which he is making reference, so that I can provide him with an appropriate answer.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Yesterday, the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock put a question. The minister gave an answer. It was the hon. member's impression that the minister's answer excluded

the area on which the hon. member was concentrating. I allowed the point of order today to clarify whose impression was correct as to the response given by the hon. minister. speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: TRANSPORT-INCENTIVES FOR NEW GRAIN TERMINAL FACILITIES AT CANADIAN PORTS
speechtext: The government is aware of the Canadian Wheat Board's incentive program to encourage construction of new grain terminal facilities at West Coast ports. Any money required for the program would come from the Board's pool accounts, as a deduction from final payment monies. Under the main provisions of the program, companies building terminal facilities at Canadian West Coast ports will be guaranteed storage payments on 90 to 100 per cent of their total licensed capacity less a minimum of 10 per cent which they must reserve for non-Board grains. The payments which will be set at the present storage rate, of one-thirtieth of a cent per bushel per day, will represent additional expenses to pool accounts only for that portion of storage capacity which goes unutilized. In other words to the extent that the storage capacity is fully utilized to store grain, the incentive program would not represent any additional expense to the board's pool accounts.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I begin by thanking the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes) for his courtesy in allowing me to speak first on Bill C-9 at this stage of the proceedings. The courtesy displayed by the hon. member this afternoon is typical of the atmosphere which prevailed through the long and very detailed hearings we had at the committee stage of this bill.
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-9 which is now before the House for third reading is the result of 5 Vi years of discussions and negotiations among the Crees and the Inuit of northern Quebec, the federal government and the provincial government of Quebec. It has been a long journey. But what was happening during those years was far more than the seeking of a concession here, or a gain there which the word "negotiation" often implies. It was nothing less that an attempt to fit together, in a new and lasting way, two different cultures and lifestyles, two different sets of priorities, and to fit them together in a way that would accommodate both groups in the pursuit of their own interests without infringing on the basic rights and responsibilities of each. This was no small undertaking, it was no easy task, and I believe that the success attained represents a monumental achievement.
It was Quebec's intention to develop the hydroelectric potential of the James Bay region that precipitated the negotiations which would lead to the James Bay and Northern Quebec
80012 -56Vi

May 4, 1977
James Bay Agreement
Agreement. Prior to that time, the government of Canada, the government of Quebec, and the Indians of Quebec Association, had formed a tripartite committee-that was in 1969-to deal with general problems related to harvesting and other questions of concern to the native population. But with the announcement of the proposed hydroelectric project, the Cree people living in the area became aware of the urgency of a settlement of their claims and reacted by asking the federal government to ensure that such settlement was reached before the project was allowed to develop further.
Indeed, both the provincial and federal governments had certain obligations with respect to the settlement of native claims in the territory where the projects would be located. The terms of the Quebec Boundaries Extension Act of 1912, which transferred the area north of the Eastmain River from the Northwest Territories to Quebec jurisdiction provided that the province would recognize native rights in that area and pay compensation for the surrender of such rights in the same manner as the government of Canada had previously done in other areas. With the federal government lay the broader responsibility for Indian and Inuit people, as expressed in the BNA Act and subsequent legislation, including the Indian Act.
By virtue of this responsibility, the federal government made repeated attempts to convince the province of the necessity of a negotiated settlement and to regenerate tripartite discussions. The federal government also provided funds to the Crees, through the Indians of Quebec Association, to assist them in informing their people of the proposed development and in conducting research on their claim. In 1972, when the natives felt negotiations with Quebec were not progressing favourably, they decided to launch a court action in an attempt to halt the project. The federal government, in an effort to bring the province to the negotiating table, provided the Crees and Inuit with financial assistance.
While the parties awaited the judgment of Justice Albert Malouf on the natives' request for an interlocutory injunction to stop the project, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Allmand), continued to urge the province to resume negotiations and suggested a number of components for a possible settlement, which were included in Premier Bourassa's offer of January 25, 1974, and ultimately became the basis of the agreement in principle signed on November 15, 1974.
I firmly believe, now that Bill C-9 is before us for third reading, that the agreement that will be put into effect by this legislation is worthy of the efforts that were made by all parties involved to reach an accommodation and to produce a lasting settlement. What the agreement does is to acknowledge the traditional use and occupancy of the land by the Crees and Inuit of northern Quebec, and to provide, in place of general, unspecified interest in the land-which had never been sanctioned or protected by treaties or laws in that territory- concrete, well-defined rights and benefits to be given legal status by the passage of Bill C-9.
In its 1973 policy statement on native claims, the federal government formally recognized the existence of a native
[Mr. Pcnner.)
usufructuary interest in areas of Canada where it had not been extinguished by treaty or superseded by law-and that included the area of northern Quebec covered by the Boundaries Extension Acts of 1898 and 1912. In making that statement, the government clearly acknowledged its willingness to negotiate with Indian and Inuit representatives an agreed form of compensation on the basis of the loss of that interest. The James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement is the first comprehensive claim settlement resulting from negotiations based on this policy.
During the many months of discussions and negotiations of the James Bay claim, the federal government recognized that the concern of the native people in the area was not primarily for obtaining monetary compensation but, rather, for preserving their traditional culture and gaining an effective voice in controlling matters affecting their daily lives in the territory. The wish of the federal government was to see the provision of nothing less than a new economic, social and cultural framework for the native people of the territory which would strengthen their position in contemporary society and at the same time enable them to set their own goals and to reach those goals in their own way and their own time. The concern of the government here today is to see the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement, which provides that framework, enshrined in legislation enacted by this parliament and given the finality and binding force of law.
What the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement has done, in short, is to meet the expressed needs of the Crees and Inuit of the territory with respect to the usage and occupancy of lands, special hunting, fishing and trapping arrangements, health and social services, education, the administration of justice, economic development opportunities, protection of the environment, and local and regional autonomy.

There is not much left.
Mr. Pennen The hon. member says there is not much left. He is absolutely correct. This agreement is very comprehensive. It has looked at every area of concern and interest to the Crees and Inuit and covered them all very comprehensively. I thank the hon. member for his interjection.
The agreement will result in greater control by the native people of their own affairs and increased native participation in all aspects of the administration of the territory, thereby reducing their dependence on government and making a positive move away from the paternalism of the past. In years gone by the federal government has frequently been criticized in this regard. This increased native autonomy should not be interpreted as an attempt on the part of the federal government to abrogate its responsibilities for native people. In addition to the specific rights and benefits outlined in the agreement, Bill C-9 ensures that the native people in the territory will continue to enjoy the rights and benefits resulting from the Indian Act where applicable and from such special legislation as may flow from the agreement at a future date. The Cree and Inuit will also continue to benefit from general federal and provincial programs applicable to Indians and
May 4, 1977

Inuit in Canada and in Quebec. They will, of course, continue to enjoy the same rights as other Canadian citizens. That goes without saying.
Perhaps the most important aspect of the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement is that it was designed in such a way as to allow for accommodation. It represents an honest attempt by all signatory parties to accommodate particular needs and fulfil particular obligations in a manner satisfactory to all concerned. It is regarded by the participants as a good settlement, not as a model for others, for which it is not meant, but one to be defended in terms of the mutual satisfaction and benefits it brings to those who signed it.
In signing the agreement, the native people have agreed to the surrender of their claims in the territory, and also to the continuation of the James Bay hydroelectric project, in consideration of the benefits they will receive under the agreement. Quebec, for its part, has made certain modifications to its original plans for the hydro project as a result of the natives' concerns and will also undertake remedial measures to minimize, to the greatest extent possible, damages to the natives' way of life resulting from the project.
Numerous other examples of accommodation can be found in every section of the agreement. Arrangements have been worked out for land use in the territory, with defined categories of land to be established for the native people, and special provisions for non-native purposes. In recognition of the expressed needs of the Cree people, the federal government has agreed to give them local by-law powers more extensive than those accorded to bands under the Indian Act. The Province, for its part, will incorporate all the Cree and Inuit communities as municipalities under Quebec law, and has agreed to make arrangements for increased native participation in the administration of the territory. This will be done, for example, by creating new structures for the administration of Cree and Inuit health and education. In other areas, such as policing and judicial administration, existing provincial structures and programs will be adapted to make room for native participation and to take into account the unique concerns of the Cree and Inuit people. Under the agreement, both governments have agreed to Cree and Inuit involvement in the processes for environmental and social protection and in the management of the hunting, fishing and trapping regime in the territory.
Quebec is also offering added incentives to those natives who wish to pursue their traditional way of life, in the form of a guaranteed annual income program for Cree hunters and trappers and an income support program for disadvantaged Inuit. The federal and provincial governments have also undertaken, within the scope of existing programs, to provide training and other assistance for economic development, which will be consistent with the special needs of the Cree and Inuit. In addition, the natives will be given the opportunity to obtain jobs within the government service and on government development projects in the territory.
James Bay Agreement
From the examples I have given, it is clear that the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement is the result of significant compromises and adaptation by all parties involved. But the agreement does not stop there. It has opened the door for other native people in Quebec and elsewhere who are not entitled to benefit from its provisions but who may have claims in the territory. It assures them of a chance to obtain certain rights and benefits which otherwise they might not have had.
Under paragraph 2.14 of the agreement, Quebec has undertaken to negotiate with other Indians and Inuit concerning any claims they may be able to establish with respect to the territory. Questions were asked during the debate on second reading and throughout the standing committee hearings with respect to other native groups not parties to the agreement whose interests in the territory will be extinguished by Bill C-9. I should like to reiterate that in the view of the federal government, paragraph 2.14 protects non-signatory natives who can establish valid claims to land in the territory. It constitutes a legal and contractual obligation which the province has stated it fully intends to honour.
In his inaugural address before the National Assembly on March 8, Premier Levesque confirmed this very intention. Quebec's participation in the negotiations with the Naskapis of Schefferville, which are now nearing completion, is a concrete example of its willingness to negotiate, pursuant to paragraph 2.14, with natives not party to the agreement.
In conclusion, I reiterate the firm belief of the federal government that the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement represents a major development in the relationship between governments and the native people concerned. I am convinced that it is a good agreement, for it is the result of long and careful negotiations which were aimed at reaching a settlement that would truly meet the special needs of the Cree and Inuit in northern Quebec. In their testimony before the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the native parties to the agreement made it quite clear that they, too, feel the agreement is a good one.
But this agreement will come into effect officially only upon proclamation of the federal and provincial legislation approving it. Until the adoption of Bill C-9, the provisions of the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement cannot be fully implemented and the Cree and Inuit cannot enjoy the full benefits to which they are entitled as a result of this agreement. It is understandable, therefore, that the native parties are anxious to see Bill C-9 adopted. I recommend, therefore, that Bill C-9 receive third reading as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on Bill C-9 which has been before the House and the standing committee for some time. At the outset, let me refer to the Naskapis of Schefferville. As I said in the House when this bill was debated last week at the report stage, the Naskapis and their legal counsel were concerned about the terms under which this matter was to be debated at third reading. The minister made a commitment, if they were not happy with the terms under which this matter was to proceed to third reading, to defer third reading for at least a month. I

May 4, 1977
James Bay Agreement
am satisfied that the Naskapis and their legal counsel are pleased to see this matter being debated today on third reading.
While on the subject of the Naskapis, I should mention that we on this side of the House feel that we can take much credit for what has come out of the negotiations with the Naskapis at Schefferville. I suggest that the same can be said of problems which arose at Port Burwell and other issues relating to Indian, Metis and native individuals within and outside the territory involved.
I shall emphasize today, as I said during the second reading debate, during standing committee hearings and during the report stage debate, that the major issue confronting us is the extinguishment of third parties, or non-signatories to the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement. Although I have had personal reservations about the James Bay agreement, which I have read and reread, I want to say that at all times I have respected the position of the Grand Council of the Cree and their chief, Billy Diamond. I respected the chief as well as the position of the president of the Northern Quebec Inuit Association, Charlie Watt.
At no time did I feel parochial or paternalistic in terms of the content of the agreement. 1 want to remind all members of this House that that was not the issue. The issue was not the content of the agreement. The issue was the unilateral extinguishment of the rights of native people, whether they be Indian, Inuit or Metis, in that area who may or may not have rights. That was the particular issue before the House and the standing committee. Let me attempt to put it very simply, because it is most important that all members understand precisely what we are dealing with. Where is the justice in a government saying to a group of Indians, "We recognize that you have certain rights, which we will extinguish for other rights?"-rights that will appear in this agreement-and saying to another group of Indians or Inuit in the area, "You may or may not have rights, but it does not really matter because we plan on extinguishment unilaterally". That was the major contention throughout this entire debate.
As I have indicated, I had some reservations about the agreement. One of the fears that I expressed during second reading debate concerned the constitutional responsibility of the federal government. I raised that matter because I was interested in a television news broadcast last night in which the chief of the Grand Council of the Cree, Billy Diamond, raised fears with regard to the introduction of Bill 1 in the province of Quebec. It is my understanding-I think the parliamentary secretary referred to this fact-that they have asked for a delay in the proclamation of that bill in the hope that this particular aspect of the agreement can be worked out.
As I have indicated, I did not during the standing committee meetings deal in depth with the agreement, although I had read it on many occasions. I think it is important to refer to the particular clause. Under the Cree education act, section 16.0.10 states specifically:

The teaching languages shall be Cree and with respect to the other languages in accordance with the present practice in the Cree communities in the territory. The Cree School Board will pursue as an objective the use of French as a language of instruction so that pupils graduating from its schools will, in the future, be capable of continuing their studies in a French school, college or university elsewhere in Quebec, if they so desire.
After consultation with the parents' committee, and having regard to the requirements of subsequent education, the commissioners shall determine the rate of introduction of French and English as teaching languages.
I do not pretend to be a constitutional expert, but it is certainly the view of the Grand Council of the Cree-indeed, Charlie Watt of the Northern Quebec Inuit Association made reference to it-that we may well see the erosion of the agreement. I referred to this matter during the second reading debate, and I want to make reference to that particular section. In Hansard for December 7, 1976, at page 1760 I am reported as having said:
On November 6, 1975, an article appeared in the Montreal Gazette describing certain features of the agreement. In that article the MNA for Mount Royal, John Ciacca, who served as the provincial government negotiator, stated:
In effect the agreement will have precedence over the federal Indian Act...
It is our end to create a new concept within the framework of a Quebec lawthe establishment of a community lived in either by Cree or Inuit of their own
choice but also accessible to the rest of the population.
As I indicated at that time, that was certainly my understanding of the agreement, an entirely new concept with respect to constitutional responsibility. There was nor question throughout the testimony that that particular section 16.0.10 was of extreme importance to the Cree as, indeed, were other sections. It is incumbent upon this government and this minister that that section should be defended. There is no question about that. It is important to recall the major arguments throughout the standing committee meetings. They really revolve around sections 2.6 and 2.14. As I have indicated, that was repeated throughout the testimony.
There are several areas I could refer to with regard to section 2.14. I want to make reference to the meeting that was held on Tuesday, March 8, 1977. It clearly defines the issue as we on this side of the House saw it. At page 21:34 of issue No. 21 for Tuesday, March 8, 1977, the testimony is as follows. I asked the following question:
Well, now that we have legal counsel here, let me put a question to him, through you, Mr. Chairman, if I may.
How comfortable would legal counsel be, if they were in the position of a third party who may or may not have third rights, when you are confronted with a bill that extensively extinguishes the rights of third parties or non-signatories to the agreement? What leverage do you have as a third party to negotiate when your rights are extinguished before you start?
The witness from the Department of Justice responded:
Well, I would say that all that this third party can do would be to rely on the good faith of the Quebec government that undertook to negotiate, presumably in good faith, with anybody who has a claim. And that is all the person can do.
I then said:
A moral obligation but no legal obligation.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Allmand) interrupted at that point and said:
Oh no, there is a legal obligation to negotiate but no legal obligation to settle.
May 4, 1977

That is the crux of the problem that was before the committee. In a sense, they were saying there was a moral obligation but no legal obligation. I say that that legal obligation was extinguished by section 3(3) of the bill that was before us and which we were trying to correct by the amendment which was defeated earlier this afternoon. When I spoke on second reading, I indicated that this was a key issue. I refer again to that debate, and specifically to page 1764 of Hansard for December 7, 1976. I stated at that time:
I want to emphasize that any approach to the resolution of native problems in our democratic society must be based on the fundamental principle that all Canadians will benefit by supporting the development of a pluralistic culture in which the culture of the native people, as indeed of other minorities, will have an opportunity to grow and develop.
That is the crux of the issue. The parliamentary secretary is quite correct when he says that the Grand Council of Cree and the Northern Quebec Inuit Association made eloquent presentations and were quite prepared to proceed with the bill. But I would point out to him that there are numerous people in that area who did not sign the agreement and whose rights were extinguished unilaterally. They will have no legal position from which to negotiate in the future.
I have no intention of reviewing the numerous ramifications of the bill and of the agreement, but I wish to make a few further observations before returning to the subject of non-signatories. I think it was obvious from the outset when we discussed these matters in committee that we were talking about people and about opportunity for the development of their lifestyles. Let me give hon. members an example taken from numerous illustrations which were given throughout the testimony. I think it will exemplify the mood of the hearings. On Thursday, February 10, 1977, as reported in issue No. 12, representatives of the Labrador Inuit Association appeared before the standing committee. I should like to refer to page 12 A1 of the report of the proceedings and to the comments made by Jerry Sillitt, an Inuit from Nain, Labrador. I quote from his presentation:
I will tell a little of what I remember concerning our land. In those days I was able to go with hunters when they went hunting for caribou or foxes. In those days we would follow the animals. Some winters caribou and foxes would be handier than other winters for animals move constantly and have to be followed. We would have to go further in the country. Sometimes we would be out in the country for two months and a half and sometimes even three if we and the dogs had food. If there were no animals we would come back empty handed, before our dogs starved. These past years, it was not difficult to get caribou. This winter it is doubtful where there might be caribou close by. That is why when the weather clears up and when the days are longer, the hunters will surely go hunting for Quebec was included in Labrador country because we would go beyond the border to hunt for our food and food for our dogs in earlier years and they have to go there again.
That is the kind of testimony we heard repeatedly throughout the sittings-conclusive evidence of the way of life the Indians, Inuit and non-status individuals have pursued from time immemorial. Yet the government has taken the position that the rights of these people should be extinguished, with the result that they will be deprived of any legal basis for a settlement in the future. I could have quoted numerous pas-
Jantes Bay Agreement
sages from other testimony to illustrate the lifestyle followed by these people and the importance of the land to them.
The parliamentary secretary referred to the long period during which the negotiations were carried on with respect to the James Bay agreement. Let me remind you, Mr. Speaker, that the James Bay project was announced in 1971 without reference to the native people. They were not consulted. The federal government chose to ignore the situation. The government failed to discharge its constitutional responsibility in this area. It preferred to take an attitude of "alert neutrality": this was the term they used. Imagine the Indians and the Inuit negotiating opposite the government of Quebec, Quebec Hydro and the James Bay Development Corporation. Imagine the odds in a situation like that! Nevertheless, the federal government, despite its obligations of trust toward these people, stood silently by.
I commend the Cree and the Northern Quebec Inuit Association for obtaining some of the things they did. But let us be realistic. They were negotiating with a gun to their head. They were obliged to operate within a restricted time-frame. Then, again, they were obliged to negotiate in Montreal. Here are Inuit from the Arctic circle, Cree from the interior of Quebec, unfamiliar with an urban environment as we know it, yet brought down to a big, modern city to negotiate in what, for them, might be termed a hostile environment.
I should like to refer again to what I consider to be the key issue in this debate, that is, the third parties or non-signatories to the agreement. It is important that hon. members should clearly understand the magnitude of this problem and the injustice which will be perpetrated by the passage of the bill in its present form. During the report stage I referred to the fact that the Grand Council of the Cree, and even their legal counsel and their chief, when they were making strong representations before the committee in favour of the quick passage of this bill, agreed that the approach was not an ideal one. I want to refer to issue No. 6 of the committee report dated June 25, 1977. I invite hon. members to turn to the testimony which was given by Mr. O'Reilly, legal counsel for the Grand Council of the Cree. He said:
There is no question as to what is being done. I think the stakes are high for every native group which is involved. There is no question that the stakes are also very high for the governments and the Crown Corporations and the other Indians who are involved. The idea is, in effect, to wipe the slate clean over a definite geographic area. There is no question that it is preferable that everybody and anybody who has any interest whatsoever in that full geographic area should be party to the agreement. That would have been the preference; that would have been the best thing. But that would have involved perhaps 20 or 25 groups.
He went on to say that that is the dilemma with which Canada is faced, that it is not a precedent which is a happy one. Let me assure you, Mr. Speaker that it certainly is not a precedent which is a happy one. The injustice of this particular action is so obvious to those who attended throughout the standing committee hearings and to anyone who has studied the agreement and this legislation. Then on February 3, the Northern Quebec Inuit Association appeared before the committee and the president gave testimony. What he said regard-

May 4, 1977
James Bay Agreement
ing the third parties and non-signatories was very revealing. Let me quote at page 9:15 what the president of the Quebec Inuit Association had to say:
To answer your question about extinguishment of rights of third parties, about third parties, we have never been completely satisfied with the compensation of the surrender, of the extinguishment of our rights, and we ourselves do not have any authority to extinguish rights of other groups.
The federal government is the only body that has the authority to cause surrender. The surrender and extinguishment of rights is not something that we dispense. We do not have that authority. It is the federal government that has the job of extinguishing rights.
That was the crux of the issue, Mr. Speaker. The federal government had the trust and responsibility on behalf of the Indian and native peoples. It had the constitutional responsibility under the British North America Act. Yet it abrogated that responsibility by unilaterally extinguishing the rights of a large number of Indian and native peoples in that territory.
On February 10, the Labrador Inuit Association appeared before the committee, and I referred earlier to some of the testimony given by one of the Inuit of Nain who appeared. At page 12A:10 of the standing committee meeting this was said with reference to third parties and non-signatories to the agreement:
The intention of clause 3(3) seems to be clear: the aboriginal and statutory rights of the Inuit and Indians whether or not they are ordinarily resident in Quebec in and to the territory, and whether or not they are beneficiaries under the agreement, are to be abrogated.
This has significance not only for those Inuit, Naskapi and Montagnais Innu of Labrador and the Schefferville Naskapi. It has significance for all Canadians because this clause raises serious and disturbing questions about the political integrity of the government and of parliament.
We think it important to bring to the attention of this standing committee one or two items which the government appears to have overlooked. These relate to the political history of the land rights issue and the legal history of the territory.
They then went on to talk about the breach of faith on the part of the federal government respecting the commitment that was made by the former minister in August, 1973. These people represented by the Labrador Inuit Association have had traditional rights in that area from time immemorial, rights which are being unilaterally extinguished by this government.
Then on February 10, 1977, in issue No. 13 of the proceedings of the committee, we have the testimony of the Naskapi Montagnais Innu Association of Labrador. I want to refer to some testimony which indicates their concern about the legislation before us, as well as their concern at the unilateral extinguishment of third party rights. In a letter which was sent to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development on October 27, 1976, which is to be found at page 13A:20 of the proceedings, they had this to say:
Over the past nine months, representatives of the Naskapi-Montagnais Innu Association have corresponded with the governments of Canada, Quebec, and Newfoundland in an effort to bring about negotiations related to the interests of Labrador Indians in Quebec. In a letter written to your predecessor, the Honourable Judd Buchanan, on May 12, 1976, we expressed our concern that negotiations concerning our interests in Quebec be entered into before passage of the enabling legislation for the James Bay Agreement, which will extinguish all rights for Indians and Inuit in the territory of northern Quebec. Mr. Buchanan referred us, on June 28, 1976, to section 2.14 of the James Bay Agreement, and stated that Quebec's undertaking to negotiate with other Indians and Inuit should alleviate our concerns with respect to the eventual passage of the James Bay legislation. Despite Mr. Buchanan's assurances, we remain deeply con-
(Mr. Holmes.)
cerned because, in our view, once the enabling legislation is passed extinguishing all rights, there is no guarantee as to what kind of agreement the government of Quebec will arrive at with us, even if negotiations do take place. Furthermore, section 2.14 concludes with the sentence, "This paragraph shall not be enacted into law''. Therefore, there is no legal requirement for Quebec to enter into negotiations.
I could cite additional testimony given by the Naskapi Montagnais Innu Association of Labrador, but here is another group of individuals, so-called third parties and non-signatories to this agreement, who are being ignored by the government. The National Indian Brotherhood appeared before the standing committee on February 15, 1977, and I read into the record at report stage this past week their principal concern regarding the legislation now before the House, which was the rights of third parties or nonsignatories to the agreement. Although they expressed other concerns, that was the major one. They pleaded before the standing committee that the government of Canada reverse its position in terms of extinguishing the rights of third parties.
Then on February 17 the ITC appeared before the standing committee and principally made representations from the settlements of Povungnituk, Ivujivik and Sugluk. The concerns of Inuit communities respecting this agreement are still not yet resolved. I received a letter as recently as April 15 of this year from the Inuit Community Council at Sugluk expressing their concern, and I should like to read part of it into the record because I think it is most important:
We are writing now for we were going to write to you here from Sugluk.
While you were here you spoke about the islands wanting to negotiate with the federal government. Also that you are going to try to have the support of the federal government to take the islands. This is the follow-up of what you said.
We cannot go with the agreement. We want Charlie Watt to tell both governments, federal and provincial, that we cannot be included in the agreement because we are not going with any of the agreements as people of Sugluk. We also are not included in the Bill C-9. We cannot give up what power we have. We have been living here for ages and we cannot give up what our fathers worked so hard for. We just cannot sell our ways and life because this is all very valuable to us. We cannot exchange our land for money. We will not let this land go just for money.
I could go on, but the point I am making, despite the comments of the parliamentary secretary, is that the problem is not yet resolved. This is an incident concerning the injustice to third parties, or non-signatories. I received a copy of a letter dated April 15. They have been excluded, by this government, in the legislation before us. I see my time is running out.
You have unlimited time.

Thank you, Stanley. On February 22, 1977, the Naskapis Indians of Schefferville appeared before us. As I indicated earlier, we have indications that the agreements are proceeding. I also pointed out that we on this side of the House take a lot of credit for those negotiations. It took a lot of prodding of the government to get them to a stage where there may well be an agreement somewhere along the line. They made an excellent presentation regarding the injustices to third parties and non-signatories to the agreement.

On Wednesday, February 23, 1977, we had the Inuit Tapisi-rat of Canada. As I indicated previously, they made a very strong presentation regarding third party rights. Referring to issue No. 17 of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the testimony of the witness at page 17:9-the witness was the director of the land claims project for the Inuit Tapisirat of Canada-stated, in reference to the problems identified with ITN:
We cannot really blame the people from those three communities in Northern Quebec, Povungnituk, Ivujivik and Sugluk for objecting to the type of agreement that was reached because to their minds it was not a very good settlement. It was made under pressure from Hydro Quebec and those developers, and as far as we are concerned, those developers, Hydro Quebec and those other groups, really had no right in being part of the negotiations. The agreement should have been between the Inuit people and the Government of Canada and perhaps the provincial government, but as far as we are concerned, Hydro Quebec, James Bay Development Corporation and all those different private interests had no right in taking part in the agreement. It should have been an agreement between the Inuit and the government-
This was a contention we had made. The federal government took a position of alert neutrality throughout the entire negotiation and, of course, abrogated their responsibilities. On February 24, 1977, the Native Council of Canada made a strong presentation. The president of the Native Council of Canada, as reported at page 18:4, indicated the following:
The bill will eliminate all native rights for all native people for all time in the area covered by the agreement. Thousands of native families who are neither Indian nor Inuit, who are not under the umbrella of a special federal department but who also live on these lands and whose traditional livelihood is equally threatened, have no safeguards under the proposed agreement.
At the same time, similar testimony was received from the Laurentian Alliance of Metis and Non-Status Indians by the president, Mr. Carl Lariviere. The testimony overwhelmingly demonstrates the injustice of ignoring Indians, Inuit, Metis and non-status Indians in the particular agreement.
On March 1, 1977, le Conseil Attikamek-Montagnais made a very excellent presentation before the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I will not quote from this particular one, but it pointed out very clearly the injustice that was being created by section 3.3 of the agreement which effectively unilaterally would extinguish the rights of all of those with the exception of the Cree and the Inuit. On Thursday, March 3, 1977, the Abitibi dominion band council made a similar presentation and again demonstrated that they, and others in the area, would have their rights extinguished unilaterally by the legislation that is before us.
The testimony we have seen in the standing committee meeting is, in my view, self-explanatory. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the government have ignored and abrogated their responsibilities with respect to the people in that area. They have unilaterally extinguished the rights of the Indian, Inuit and native peoples. That is action which cannot be justified on human grounds, and action-as I indicated throughout the debate on second reading and the standing committee hearings-which I cannot support.

Mr. Speaker, because of the hon. member's reference to the minister's statement that a legal commitment
James Bay Agreement
on the part of the province of Quebec existed to negotiate, but did not exist to settle third party claims, and because the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes) implied that there would be an end to any possible recourse for such third party claims, I just want to ask the hon. member: Does he not agree that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, at more than one point in the committee proceedings, went on record to the effect that in the unlikely event that such third party claims were not negotiated by the province in good faith, it was declared federal policy to negotiate and settle any legitimate third party claim? In fairness, I think this should be on the record.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member raises a question which was thoroughly debated and discussed at the standing committee hearings. What he is implying in his question is an issue we have raised many times. When you assess the agreement and the legislation, you will see there is only a moral commitment on the part of the federal government and the provincial governments involved. We have demonstrated very clearly in the legislation and the agreement before us that there is a commitment to negotiate, but there is not a commitment to settle. The rights they had have been unilaterally extinguished. How can you trade if you have nothing to trade with, if those rights have been extinguished unilaterally?
The hon. member is saying that there is a moral agreement on the part of the minister that if there is no action, he will take action. The record of the government, in terms of moral commitment to the Indian and Inuit people of this country, has been deplorable. We cannot support legislation that simply gives credence to a moral principle rather than a legal principle.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I will not take much time of the House on the bill that is before us today. It is a shame that it even exists and that we are wasting our time on it in the House. I will not take much time on it; I have only a few words to say about the bill. If I had better words to say about it, perhaps I would take a little more time of the House.
Earlier in the debate on Bill C-9 I voiced strenuous objection to the bill. I did so during second reading of this legislation last December. I said at that time that I could not support Bill C-9 as it then stood. After several months of discussion in committee, of hearing many witnesses and many groups before the committee expressing their views on the bill, and after some small changes had been made to the bill, I am still of the same opinion that I cannot support it. I, and my colleagues of the NDP, do not want to be blamed in history for such bad legislation. 1 cannot support the bill mainly because of clause 3, which provides in part:
3(3) All native claims, rights, title and interests, whatever they may be, in and to the territory, of all Indians and all Inuit, wherever they may be... are hereby extinguished,

May 4, 1977
James Bay Agreement
I cannot support that. I hoped when I was first elected to the House a few years ago that I would be in a position to support some good legislation concerning native rights, that I would see a better bill brought forward that would enshrine in the BNA Act the aboriginal rights of the native population of Canada. It is obvious to me that Bill C-9 is in no way an improvement on earlier treaties between the native people and the government. The intent of the bill is pretty well the same as that of other treaties agreed upon by the Indians and the government in the last century and the early part of this century. The government agrees to pay $225 million to the native people in the James Bay area listed in the agreement covered by the bill. This is what an Indian and Inuit will get for signing away his aboriginal rights forever. The cash settlement amounts to approximately $1,000 per year per person. That is why I have referred to this in the past as a modern-day treaty.
In the earlier treaties the Canadian government paid around $5 per person per year. The going rate today seems to be $1,000. While the government may take into consideration such modern-day phenomena as inflation, whether the government pays $5 or $ 1,000, the terms are still the same; and I say they are not for the good of the native people. Who benefits from this treaty? It is mostly the government of Quebec and Hydro Quebec who are the beneficiaries, because in the long run they will win, while the native people will get the wrong end of the deal.
The very basis of this agreement is that it deals with the rights of native people. This agreement deals with native rights as they relate to land-land which the native people have inhabited since time immemorial. This is one of the concepts that seems difficult for the white man to understand, that is, the Indian people's understanding of land ownership. There is a situation in the Northwest Territories where two treaties were signed some 50 or 60 years ago, and the land question has not been settled yet because the treaties say that the Indian people are entitled to one square mile of land for every five people, or some such formula.
The Indian people do not accept the concept of ownership of land where you have a certificate which says the land is yours. Their understanding of it is not the same as that of most other people. For the Indians, one square mile of land for five people would be a very bad situation, and that is why it has not been accepted generally and the matter has not been settled in the Northwest Territories. An Indian family who lives off the land needs hundreds of square miles. For example, there is a certain time of the year when they go to the fishing grounds. The fishing grounds take up many square miles of land and many square miles of water.
At another time of the year they go to another part of the country to hunt caribou, and caribou need hundreds of square miles of land to survive. This is the main supply of food and clothing for the Indians. There is another time of the year when the Indians go to berry growing grounds. Again that takes up hundreds of square miles. When you realize that those people depend on the land for their livelihood, you also
[Mr. Firth.J
realize how precious those lands are to them; and when you see a document in which people give up their aboriginal rights for a few dollars, it is very sad. By seeking to extinguish these rights and claims to the land, the government is, in effect, conceding that these rights and claims to the land exist in the first place. These claims are very real.
The native people of Canada lived and died on lands covered by this agreement long before the white man ever discovered them. There is an interesting point here that I would like to make. I think the white man should ask himself why the Indian people have been fighting for centuries to survive as a group and to conserve their culture, even after 400 years of oppression by the government, by trading companies, by churches and by the general public. As a matter of fact, that was indicated a little while ago in the report of the RCMP. We have been oppressed by that group, also, for a long time. In a recent report of the RCMP to the government it was stated that the greatest threat to the security of this nation are the native people of Canada. This is a ridiculous statement. When we ask ourselves why, even after all these years of oppression, the Indians are still trying to keep their culture, we find that there must be a good reason for this. That is something to think about.
I refer to the James Bay agreement as a modern-day treaty. I would like to say, again, that I and my colleagues do not want to be blamed in history for supporting such a bill. I relate it to the signing of earlier treaties by the government with the native people of this country. You do not hear people say that the chiefs who signed these earlier treaties are heros of this country nor do you see any monuments to them. I think most of them feel sad about having signed the treaties in the first place. Therefore, in no way can I support Bill C-9.
[DOT] (noo)
When we look at some of the guarantees provided in the bill, such as the hunting and trapping rights for people of the area, we remember that the hunting grounds are flooded and are subject to mercury and all kinds of pollution from industry. The experience of the Northwest Territories in respect to employment from these projects has not been good. Imperial Oil has been operating at Norman Wells for about 40 years, pumping oil and gas, but I know of only one native person who is a full-time employee of the company. The oil was discovered by a native person who did not receive any benefit from it.
Another example is the gas pipeline at Pointed Mountain near the settlement of Fort Liard in the Northwest Territories which was built four or five years ago without a single job going to a native person. Development of lands by big industry has not always benefited the native people. I am, therefore, opposed to Bill C-9 and in particular to clause 3(3) regarding the extinguishment of aboriginal rights. I feel that the Canadian government failed to live up to its responsibilities to the native peoples in the negotiations.
For the Cree, it is a modern-day treaty, with many fine benefits that other Indian groups never received, but at a tremendous price, that of forfeiting all claims and rights as an
May 4, 1977

indigenous people. This is the first agreement ever negotiated by an Inuit association with the Canadian government. I think it is a bad precedent and I would not want to see future agreements for the Inuit people along these lines.
I find that the Canadian government has had little concern for third party claimants who will be automatically affected by this agreement. This James Bay method of negotiating will soon be applied to my region-the Mackenzie Valley. I know that the Canadian government will say that it is very flexible and treats each claim on its own merits. However, the native peoples of Canada, from over four centuries of experience, know that it is always the same old policies that are applied by the government in the end.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would say that the only way the Canadian government can truly live up to its responsibilities to the native peoples under the James Bay agreement is by removing clause 3(3) of Bill C-9. Nothing less will do. As I said last December, this clause goes against the wishes of many people who are involved in the cause of fighting, working and struggling for the recognition and acceptance of the fact that the native people of this country have their aboriginal rights.
Aboriginal rights should not be extinguished by an act of the Canadian parliament. Rather, they should be enshrined in the British North America Act. I fully understand and recognize the position of the Cree and Inuit in the negotiations that led to this agreement. They had to get what they could, and the price was the extinguishment of their rights as indigenous peoples. But I think the price was too high-and the government, failed, in a most shameful manner, in permitting this to happen.
I feel that no hon. member of this House can honestly support and be a party to an agreement which extinguishes for all time the aboriginal rights of the native peoples covered under the agreement. I, personally-and I speak for my colleagues-have no wish to be blamed by history for agreeing to such a treaty. But other members have their own conscience to follow.

Mr. Speaker, on April 30, 1971, the Quebec government officially announced the James Bay hydroelectric development without having consulted the people-yet repercussions would be direct-and without having studied the magnitude of its effects. It goes without saying that no study had been made, or precautions taken, with regard to the ecology or environment of the area concerned. During the following summer, the Crees learned the news and decided to convey their objections and claims to the other Indians, and the public; they finally took the matter to the courts. That was the point in time when the celebrated James Bay Agreement was launched.
After over four years of lengthy and costly negotiations, the aboriginals and other parties concerned signed a final agreement, the last major step before the one the House will take. But as we know, all litigations have not been solved; had it not
James Bay Agreement
been for the legislative obligation of passing Bill C-9 before November 1977, the whole agreement would have been called in question again, and claims and negotiations would surely have been protracted further.
However, clause 2.9.9 of the agreement implies that any further development is not likely to be dramatic. Nevertheless, Bill C-9 does not guarantee that future negotiations on rights and privileges of third parties will come to a successful conclusion. Since they are deprived of a trump card, they fear, as they have stated before the Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development, that this might result in long and hard negotiations. Therefore, it is to be hoped that governments will keep their word and will negotiate in good faith with them. It is the main point on which Bill C-9 does not come to a formal conclusion.
Lastly, I know it would take some time to review all claims put forward by third parties about Bill C-9 but, once again, the main points were that clause 2.14 of the agreement did not provide for any obligation to negotiate, that it did not have force of law and that recommendations on that matter submitted by third parties to the federal government have not been respected. According to Mr. Bernard Mathieu, who is coordinating negotiations in Quebec City, the last issues still outstanding which have not evolved for a few months are, first, the matter of coastal islands along Quebec's western, northern and northeastern boundaries. We do not know to whom they belong and who should use them. Negotiations on that matter are going on but not at a tremendous pace. Second, although most of it has been resolved through an amendment to clause 3 of Bill C-9, the problem of Inuit in Port Burwell, still remains because, according to what little information we have been able to secure, they wish to retain some territorial rights, privileges and so on.
Third, there is also the cost of negotiations claimed by the Crees and some Inuit; they want to be reimbursed. At the beginning, governments were passing the buck to each other but now they say that no provision in the agreement forced them to reimburse the cost of negotiations after a final agreement has been signed. Once again, it is very difficult to obtain the details.
Fourth, the problem of the Naskapi from Shefferville is not completely settled. Considering that they are part of the third party to the agreement, their rights will be defined and negotiated after Bill C-9 has been passed. Once again, all third party members will have to get along without the help of the federal government to define their rights because the government did not condescend to give them the legal assistance provided for in Bill C-9, and they will probably have to be satisfied with government proposals because they do not hold many trump cards. It may be feared they will turn to courts because the matter of the James Bay Agreement having been disposed of legally speaking, they will not be able to refer to it.
Fifth, there is the problem of Category II lands. The reason for the delay in reaching an agreement is mining development.

May 4, 1977
James Bay Agreement
According to the information we could obtain, it must be decided who will benefit from titles and mining fields. It must also be determined which territories will and which ones will not be affected by the development of these mining fields. Every gain increasing mining operations will amount to a loss in terms of wildlife and environment, and the Inuit are quite anxious to preserve their heritage. Sixth, the problem of the legitimate spouse has not yet been resolved. We know that it has been going on for a long time, and since an agreement had taken place before the agreement was signed, it seems the government is not prepared to make generous concessions. Meeting the demands would have meant including in Bill C-9 a clause on the eligibility of the legitimate spouse because this will probably create problems as to whether such a spouse is eligible to benefit from the agreement.
Those are, Mr. Speaker, the main conflicts that will have to be resolved to the satisfaction of all parties concerned. The negotiations are to resume actively in May 1977, that is this month, after Bill C-9 is passed, as some hope it will be. The Inuit and particularly the third parties think that if Bill C-9 is passed before the conflicts are resolved they will be deprived of a major card in the negotiations relating to the agreement because governments will have the right to decide and natives will have no legal recourse to negotiate under more advantageous conditions. And in view of the very high cost that will be incurred by third parties in the negotiations they will have to be very cooperative. However, the Inuit have certain provisions of the agreement going for them in the event their claims are dealt with after Bill C-9 is passed.
In short, those who benefitted most from the James Bay Agreement are the Cree. Naturally, they were privileged. They were directly affected by the immediate development of the James Bay, being in the very centre of operations. They were the first to start negotiations and had more time to reach an equitable agreement. They were better structured and had the advantage of larger study subsidies and more extensive negotiations. And contrary to the other parties to the agreement they have reason to complain about the slow passage of Bill C-9, and that is, as they clearly indicated, their only immediate point of dissatisfaction. The House could not meet the wishes of that band without depriving third parties because they are still far from being satisfied. Third parties need a special status to the lands where they migrate annually to continue their ancestral traditions and meet their most normal needs. The debates on this issue are still far from being over, and after Bill C-9 is passed the James Bay Agreement will surely not be a thing of the past.
Right now, more negotiations are going on in connection with the content of the agreement. I am referring to the relocation of the LG 1 power plant; la Societe d'energie de la baie James and Quebec Hydro have decided to build this plant 23 miles away from the mouth of the La Grande river, rather than at mile 44 as agreed to in chapter 8 of the agreement. Now, if the LG 1 power plant is built 21 miles closer to the west, it will directly affect the fluctuations of the water levels. Similarly, this relocation will be a major erosion factor in

Governor Island, on which the Fort Georges community is located.
Therefore, these two large provincial organizations have undertaken, in co-operation with the Cree and other native people concerned, to move the island's residents-over 1,740 Cree and 50 Inuit-to another location at mile 5, that is 5 miles further to the east of the mouth of the La Grande river. This new settlement will be built along the river on the mainland. This means the Cree and Inuit will lose several square miles of grade 1A, IB and 11 lands. They will be settled on grade 11 lands.
According to an official of the Grand Council of the Cree in Ottawa, they are prepared to move under certain conditions, and this does not jeopardize the Agreement in any way. The Cree realize that after all, nothing will turn out to their disadvantage. However, the LG 1 power plant and the Fort Georges native community relocation project have not been finalized yet. Discussions and negotiations are still under way, although the agreement has been concluded in principle. There again, a new epic era is looming large for some people, but for others, the picture is grim and they will have to work hard.
As far as the Cree are concerned, the adoption of Bill C-9 is the initial step toward the complete fulfilment of all their educational, industrial, social and training objectives. Besides, Bill 15, passed by the Quebec Legislature, will probably set up a Cree school board shortly after Bill C-9 is adopted. It is known that that school board will be given as much authority as any other Quebec school board. The Cree school board will be the first of the many steps towards socialization, that are provided for the Cree under this agreement. If the Cree avail themselves of the advantages provided by the agreement, they will have an opportunity for better development than most other people in Quebec. They regard the James Bay Agreement as the promise of a new prosperous generation, the last issued from the North American capitalistic society.
The socialization process will be longer and costlier for the Inuit but they are eager indeed to govern themselves and train those who will enrich their people later on. The Inuit of Povungnituk, Sugluk and Ivujivik have made that quite clear before the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development was right in stating in the House on Thursday last that the dissident ITN group was not opposed to the agreement nor to Bill C-9, if we consider the mini-referendum on the agreement. In fact, they did not vote against the agreement, they did not vote at all. According to the latest information, these Inuit will not go against the agreement as long as their territories or rights are respected. They stated in the memorandum they presented to the committee that they did not want any part of the agreement or Bill C-9.
No one could fault the agreement or Bill C-9 for granting privileges or compensations to eligible and status Inuit. It is still too early to tell whether or not they will profit from these advantages but since the agreement seems to satisfy the majority we can only rejoice with them.
May 4, 1977

Their first thoughts will be to design workable structures for the organizations created by the agreement and to obtain qualified personnel in education and other fields. In education, so far the Inuit have been less favoured than the Crees and, because of this, in certain cases they will have to appoint temporarily non-Inuit in several positions. And since there is no public road giving access to their territories and since climatic and geographical conditions are disagreeable for newcomers, the manpower will be rare and costly, and they will need qualified personnel.
If the native people want to benefit from all the advantages of the agreement, one of the priorities will be to upgrade means of communication and access. For instance, James Bay workers are forbidden to take the road between Mattagami and Radisson. Only large transports and other commercial vehicles may travel on this road. The only means of communication available to other people is the plane. For the moment, this is much more costly and less practical, since people have to remain in the area for several weeks when they get there unless they want to spend all their money on hiring a private plane.
If the various governments cooperate in good faith with the native people, we shall witness the development of those other cultures which will make our society, already highly polyvalent, still more complex and varied. To govern the country will become an even more difficult and astringent task. We shall have to intensify qualifications and good faith if we want to allow everyone to become agents of liberty and tolerance. Before, when a government negotiated with the Indians, it was impossible not to fear any losses on the part of the Indians, and every time the capitalist society took action which affected the Indians, the Indians preferred to avoid any unfavourable contact with the white man.
Nowadays, the Indians have adopted another position since they realized that they would be forgotten if they continued to avoid society. What would have happened is what history has shown us: the genocide of American Indians. Now, to a certain extent, we can rest more easily: Indians and Inuit have taken the means necessary to represent themselves and to develop their future social conditions. The immediate danger is politics and politization.
However, Mr. Speaker, there are some new developments. I said earlier that Bill C-9 does not conclude the debate with Indian Affairs, Crees and Inuit and we just heard what happened yesterday. Negotiations have now been interrupted by the natives until they reach an agreement with the government of the province of Quebec concerning Bill No. 1. Mr. Charlie Watt and Chief Billy Diamond, respectively president of the ANNQ and the Grand Council of the Crees, are urging the Quebec government to amend the legislation so as not to force any binding measure upon the natives. Most of them are English speaking. They wish to learn French for practical reasons, but, as the two leaders said, if the Quebec government restricts the natives' freedom of choice as concerns language and other matters, they will turn to the federal government.
James Bay Agreement
They even declared that there could be a breach of agreement or possible separation from Quebec.
The Crees have laid charges against some mining companies and others about mercury pollution. These procedures started about two months ago. The provisions of the agreement that have been made flexible intentionally are the object of very long and serious negotiations and each party interprets these clauses to its advantage. Many disputes are expected and the negotiations might come to a deadlock. Let us not believe that the passage of Bill C-9 will be the conclusion of the James Bay Agreement. When the governments said they had dropped their paternalistic attitude, they were just kidding themselves because it had been rejected by the natives. They are getting more and more greedy and we are just beginning to realize how competent, politically aggressive and ambitious they are. In the future, it will be more a question of equity and law than of good faith. Bona fide. This is why the government and the other parties concerned will have to resort to all their available competence.
Mr. Speaker, there is at present the possibility of a deadlock in a number of fields, and if no solution is found there might be legal action, which would jeopardize the whole agreement, which is the result of four years of negotiations. Caution and circumspection should not be overemphasized.
Is the House ready for the question?
Question.
Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the said motion?
Agreed.
No.
All those in favour of the motion will please say yea.
Yea.
All those opposed will please say nay.
Nay.

In my opinion the yeas have it.
And more than five members having risen:
Call in the members.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I declare the motion carried.
Bill read the third time and passed.

Mr. Speaker, this afternoon, after orders of the day, some interest was expressed in words I had meant to utter under my breath but which reached the very sensitive ears of a member opposite. Perhaps they also reached his sensitive soul. But, more unfortunately, they reached the sensitive ears of Hansard. I meant no disrespect, Mr. Speaker, and I withdraw the offensive words.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. It is the long-standing practice and tradition of the House that the word of an hon. member in such circumstances is always accepted. In line with the usual way of handling such matters, the incident is therefore closed.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: I appreciate the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: The Prime Minister insists on using profanity in the House. I think I will leave the motion on the books.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Earlier in the day the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn) raised, by way of a question of privilege, a remark of the Prime Minister. I indicated then that the matter would stand over for one day, first to give me an opportunity to verify what the words were and, of course, since the hon. member had indicated that the Prime Minister, who had then left the House, might very well want to extend an apology to the House and withdraw the remark, if that was the case obviously that would be part of the disposition I would have to make within that period of time.
I indicated that the matter would stand over, and meanwhile I will take into account the language that I see reported, and the action of the Prime Minister in the interval, in making an adjudication as to what ought to be done or how the matter ought to be handled. As I indicated earlier, I will make known that adjudication at three o'clock tomorrow.
It being after six o'clock, the House stands adjourned until two o'clock tomorrow.
At 6.41 p.m. the House adjourned, without question put, pursuant to Standing Order.

Thursday, May 5, 1977
